short: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability: four promises about transactions, kept by different parts of the system.
running each statement as its own transaction, committed as soon as it finishes. what you get without BEGIN.
a named point inside a transaction you can roll back to without losing the work before it.
a transaction after an error. it refuses every statement (25P02) until ROLLBACK, and COMMIT turns into ROLLBACK.
a session with an open transaction that isn't running a statement. it still holds its locks and its snapshot.
reading another transaction's uncommitted write. the standard allows it at READ UNCOMMITTED; postgres never does it.
reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting two values, because someone committed in between.
running the same query twice in one transaction and getting a different set of rows, because rows were inserted or deleted.
two transactions read a value, each writes back its own new value, and the second write silently replaces the first.
two reads in one transaction taken at different moments, so together they describe a state that never existed.
two transactions read the same rows, each writes a different row, and together they break a rule both checked.
every read in a transaction comes from one snapshot, and two writers can't change the same row. postgres's REPEATABLE READ.
SQLSTATE 40001: postgres aborted a transaction to keep the result correct. retry the whole transaction.
at READ COMMITTED, an UPDATE or DELETE that waited for a row re-checks its WHERE on the row's newest version.
a SELECT clause that locks the returned rows until the transaction ends. weaker forms: FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE, FOR KEY SHARE.
makes a locking read fail at once with 55P03 instead of waiting for a row someone else holds.
makes a locking read leave out rows someone else holds. the job queue clause.
no lock while reading; the UPDATE checks a version column, and UPDATE 0 means someone changed the row first.
two or more transactions each waiting for a lock another one holds. postgres cancels one with 40P01.
taking locks in one agreed order everywhere (lower id first), so waits can't form a cycle.
application code that re-runs a whole transaction after 40001 or 40P01, with a cap and a random backoff.
a lock on a number you choose, held in the lock manager but never taken by postgres for you.
